questions.prompt: A standard deck of 52 cards is shuffled. One card is drawn at random. Given that the card is red, find the probability that it is a heart.
questions.hint: There are 26 red cards in a deck. Of these, how many are hearts?
questions.explanation:
There are 26 red cards (13 hearts + 13 diamonds).

Of the 26 red cards, 13 are hearts.

P(Heart | Red) = 13/26 = 1/2

questions.prompt: Events A and B are such that P(A ∩ B) = 0.12 and P(B) = 0.4. Find P(A | B).
questions.hint: Apply the definition of conditional probability directly: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B).
questions.explanation:
Using the definition of conditional probability:

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) = 0.12 / 0.4 = 0.3

questions.prompt:
A two-way table shows the results of a survey of 100 students.

|              | Plays Sport | Does Not Play Sport | Total |
|--------------|:-----------:|:-------------------:|:-----:|
| Male         |     35      |         15          |  50   |
| Female       |     25      |         25          |  50   |
| Total        |     60      |         40          | 100   |

Find the probability that a randomly selected student plays sport, given that the student is female.
questions.hint: Restrict your attention to the Female row only. Of the 50 females, how many play sport?
questions.explanation:
Restrict to the Female row: there are 50 females in total, of whom 25 play sport.

P(Sport | Female) = 25/50 = 1/2

questions.prompt: A bag contains 5 red balls and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that the second ball is blue, given that the first ball drawn was red.
questions.hint: After removing one red ball, how many balls remain in the bag? How many of those are blue?
questions.explanation:
After drawing one red ball, the bag contains 4 red and 3 blue balls (7 balls total).

P(2nd Blue | 1st Red) = 3/7

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. Find the probability that the sum is 8, given that the first die shows a 3.
questions.hint: If the first die is 3, what value must the second die show for the sum to equal 8?
questions.explanation:
Given that the first die shows 3, the second die must show 5 for the sum to be 8.

There are 6 equally likely outcomes for the second die.

P(Sum = 8 | Die 1 = 3) = 1/6

questions.prompt: In a class of 30 students, 18 study Mathematics, 12 study Science, and 6 study both. A student is chosen at random. Find the probability that the student studies Science, given that they study Mathematics.
questions.hint: Of the 18 Mathematics students, how many also study Science?
questions.explanation:
P(Science ∩ Maths) = 6/30
P(Maths) = 18/30

P(Science | Maths) = (6/30) / (18/30) = 6/18 = 1/3

Alternatively: of the 18 Maths students, 6 also study Science, so the probability is 6/18 = 1/3.

questions.prompt: A tree diagram shows that a factory has two machines. Machine A produces 60% of items and Machine B produces 40%. The defect rate for Machine A is 3% and for Machine B is 5%. An item is selected at random and found to be defective. Find the probability that it was produced by Machine A.
questions.hint: First find P(Defective) using the law of total probability. Then apply the conditional probability formula.
questions.explanation:
P(Defective | A) = 0.03, P(A) = 0.60
P(Defective | B) = 0.05, P(B) = 0.40

P(Defective) = P(Defective | A)·P(A) + P(Defective | B)·P(B)
= (0.03)(0.60) + (0.05)(0.40)
= 0.018 + 0.020
= 0.038

P(A | Defective) = P(Defective | A)·P(A) / P(Defective)
= 0.018 / 0.038
= 18/38
= 9/19

questions.prompt: Events A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.3. Find P(A | B).
questions.hint: If two events are independent, what is the relationship between P(A | B) and P(A)?
questions.explanation:
When events A and B are independent, knowing that B has occurred does not change the probability of A.

By definition of independence: P(A | B) = P(A) = 0.5

Alternatively: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B) = 0.15 (by independence)
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = 0.15/0.3 = 0.5

questions.prompt: A jar contains 4 green and 6 yellow marbles. Three marbles are drawn one at a time without replacement. Find the probability that all three are green.
questions.hint: Use conditional probability at each stage. After each green marble is drawn, the number of green marbles and total marbles both decrease by one.
questions.explanation:
P(1st Green) = 4/10
P(2nd Green | 1st Green) = 3/9
P(3rd Green | 1st two Green) = 2/8

P(All three Green) = (4/10) × (3/9) × (2/8)
= 24/720
= 1/30

questions.prompt:
The following two-way table shows the results of a drug trial.

|              | Improved | Did Not Improve | Total |
|--------------|:--------:|:---------------:|:-----:|
| Drug         |    42    |       18        |  60   |
| Placebo      |    21    |       19        |  40   |
| Total        |    63    |       37        | 100   |

Determine whether the events 'Improved' and 'Received Drug' are independent. Justify your answer.
questions.hint: Events are independent if P(A | B) = P(A). Compare P(Improved | Drug) with P(Improved).
questions.explanation:
P(Improved | Drug) = 42/60 = 0.7
P(Improved) = 63/100 = 0.63

Since P(Improved | Drug) = 0.7 ≠ 0.63 = P(Improved), the events are not independent.

Receiving the drug increases the probability of improvement, so the events 'Improved' and 'Received Drug' are dependent.

questions.prompt: A school has 200 Year 12 students. Of these, 120 study at least one of Mathematics or English Extension. 80 study Mathematics and 70 study English Extension. A student is chosen at random from those who study Mathematics. Find the probability that this student also studies English Extension.
questions.hint: Use the inclusion-exclusion principle to find the number studying both subjects: n(M ∪ E) = n(M) + n(E) − n(M ∩ E).
questions.explanation:
Using inclusion-exclusion:
n(M ∪ E) = n(M) + n(E) − n(M ∩ E)
120 = 80 + 70 − n(M ∩ E)
n(M ∩ E) = 150 − 120 = 30

P(Eng Ext | Maths) = n(M ∩ E) / n(M) = 30/80 = 3/8

questions.prompt: Box X contains 3 red and 2 white balls. Box Y contains 1 red and 4 white balls. A fair coin is tossed: if heads, a ball is drawn from Box X; if tails, a ball is drawn from Box Y. The ball drawn is red. Find the probability that it came from Box X.
questions.hint: Use a tree diagram. Find P(Red) using the total probability rule, then apply the conditional probability formula to find P(X | Red).

questions.prompt: Events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.6, P(B | A) = 0.5, and P(B | A') = 0.2. Find P(A | B).
questions.hint: First find P(B) using the law of total probability: P(B) = P(B | A)·P(A) + P(B | A')·P(A'). Then apply the conditional probability formula.
questions.explanation:
P(A) = 0.6, so P(A') = 0.4

Find P(B) using the total probability rule:
P(B) = P(B | A)·P(A) + P(B | A')·P(A')
= (0.5)(0.6) + (0.2)(0.4)
= 0.30 + 0.08
= 0.38

Find P(A ∩ B):
P(A ∩ B) = P(B | A)·P(A) = (0.5)(0.6) = 0.30

Apply conditional probability:
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) = 0.30 / 0.38 = 30/38 = 15/19

questions.prompt: A committee of 3 is to be chosen at random from 5 men and 4 women. Find the probability that the committee contains at least one woman, given that it contains at least one man.
questions.hint: Find the number of committees with at least one man (all committees minus all-women committees). Then find how many of those also contain at least one woman (exclude all-men committees from the at-least-one-man group).
questions.explanation:
Total committees of 3 from 9 people: C(9,3) = 84

Committees with at least one man (the given condition):
= Total − (all women)
= 84 − C(4,3)
= 84 − 4
= 80

Committees with at least one man AND at least one woman (the event of interest):
= Total − (all men) − (all women)
= 84 − C(5,3) − C(4,3)
= 84 − 10 − 4
= 70

P(at least 1 woman | at least 1 man) = 70/80 = 7/8

questions.prompt: In a town, 1% of the population has a particular disease. A screening test has a 95% detection rate (it correctly identifies 95% of people who have the disease) and a 4% false positive rate (it incorrectly gives a positive result for 4% of people who do not have the disease). A randomly selected person tests positive. Find the probability that this person actually has the disease.
questions.hint: Use a tree diagram or the total probability approach. The key insight is that the base rate of the disease (1%) is very low, so even a small false positive rate produces many false positives relative to true positives.
questions.explanation:
P(Disease) = 0.01, P(No Disease) = 0.99
P(Positive | Disease) = 0.95 (detection rate)
P(Positive | No Disease) = 0.04 (false positive rate)

Find P(Positive) using the total probability rule:
P(Positive) = P(Pos | Disease) x P(Disease) + P(Pos | No Disease) x P(No Disease)
= (0.95)(0.01) + (0.04)(0.99)
= 0.0095 + 0.0396
= 0.0491

Apply conditional probability:
P(Disease | Positive) = P(Pos | Disease) x P(Disease) / P(Positive)
= 0.0095 / 0.0491
= 95/491
= 0.193 (approximately 19.3%)

Despite testing positive, there is only about a 1 in 5 chance the person actually has the disease. This counter-intuitive result occurs because the disease is rare (1%), so the small false positive rate (4%) applied to the large healthy population produces many false positives relative to the small number of true positives.

questions.prompt: Three cards are drawn without replacement from a standard deck of 52 cards. Find the probability that the third card is an ace, given that the first two cards drawn were not aces.
questions.latex: P(\text{3rd Ace} \mid \text{1st not Ace, 2nd not Ace})
questions.hint: After removing two non-ace cards, how many cards remain? How many of those are aces?
questions.explanation:
Given that the first two cards drawn were not aces, all 4 aces remain in the deck.

After removing 2 cards, there are 50 cards remaining, of which 4 are aces.

P(3rd Ace | 1st not Ace, 2nd not Ace) = 4/50 = 2/25

questions.prompt: Events A and B are such that P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, and P(A ∪ B) = 0.7. Determine whether A and B are independent, and find P(A' | B').
questions.hint: First find P(A ∩ B) using the addition rule. Check independence by testing whether P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B). For P(A' | B'), use P(A' ∩ B') = 1 − P(A ∪ B) and P(B') = 1 − P(B).
questions.explanation:
Find P(A ∩ B) using the addition rule:
P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
0.7 = 0.4 + 0.5 − P(A ∩ B)
P(A ∩ B) = 0.2

Check independence:
P(A)·P(B) = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2 = P(A ∩ B)

Since P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B), events A and B are independent.

Find P(A' | B'):
P(A' ∩ B') = P((A ∪ B)') = 1 − P(A ∪ B) = 1 − 0.7 = 0.3
P(B') = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5

P(A' | B') = P(A' ∩ B') / P(B') = 0.3 / 0.5 = 0.6

Note: Since A and B are independent, A' and B' are also independent, so P(A' | B') = P(A') = 0.6. This confirms the answer.

questions.prompt: A bag contains 10 balls numbered 1 to 10. Two balls are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that the sum of the two numbers is even, given that the larger number drawn is 7.
questions.hint: If the larger number is 7, the other number must be from {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. For the sum to be even, the other number must have the same parity as 7 (i.e. odd).
questions.explanation:
Given that the larger number is 7, the other ball must be one of {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} (each equally likely).

For the sum to be even, both numbers must have the same parity. Since 7 is odd, the other number must also be odd.

Odd numbers in {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}: {1, 3, 5} — that is 3 numbers out of 6.

P(Even Sum | Max = 7) = 3/6 = 1/2

questions.prompt: A taxi company operates in a city where 85% of taxis are green and 15% are blue. A witness to a hit-and-run accident identifies the taxi as blue. Testing shows that the witness correctly identifies the colour of a taxi 80% of the time (regardless of the actual colour). Find the probability that the taxi involved in the accident was actually blue.
questions.hint: The witness says 'blue', but witnesses are only 80% accurate. Use a tree diagram: the taxi is either blue (15%) or green (85%), and the witness identifies correctly 80% of the time in each case.
questions.explanation:
P(Blue) = 0.15, P(Green) = 0.85
P(Says Blue | Blue) = 0.80 (correct identification)
P(Says Blue | Green) = 0.20 (incorrect identification)

P(Says Blue) = P(Says Blue | Blue)·P(Blue) + P(Says Blue | Green)·P(Green)
= (0.80)(0.15) + (0.20)(0.85)
= 0.12 + 0.17
= 0.29

P(Blue | Says Blue) = P(Says Blue | Blue)·P(Blue) / P(Says Blue)
= 0.12 / 0.29
= 12/29
≈ 0.414

Despite the witness claiming the taxi was blue, there is only about a 41% chance it was actually blue. This is because green taxis are so much more common that the 20% misidentification rate applied to the large green population produces many false 'blue' reports.

questions.prompt: A company uses two stages of quality control. Stage 1 catches 90% of defective items but also incorrectly rejects 5% of non-defective items. Items that pass Stage 1 proceed to Stage 2, which catches 80% of remaining defective items but incorrectly rejects 2% of non-defective items. If 3% of all items produced are defective, find the probability that an item reaching the end of the production line (passing both stages) is defective.
questions.hint: Work through the tree diagram stage by stage. A defective item passes Stage 1 with probability 0.10, then passes Stage 2 with probability 0.20. A non-defective item passes Stage 1 with probability 0.95, then passes Stage 2 with probability 0.98.
questions.explanation:
P(Defective) = 0.03, P(Non-defective) = 0.97

Stage 1:
P(Pass S1 | Defective) = 1 - 0.90 = 0.10 (10% of defective items escape)
P(Pass S1 | Non-defective) = 1 - 0.05 = 0.95 (95% of good items pass correctly)

Stage 2 (applied only to items that passed Stage 1):
P(Pass S2 | Defective that passed S1) = 1 - 0.80 = 0.20 (20% of remaining defectives escape)
P(Pass S2 | Non-defective that passed S1) = 1 - 0.02 = 0.98 (98% of good items pass correctly)

Combined probability of passing both stages:
P(Passes Both | Defective) = 0.10 x 0.20 = 0.02
P(Passes Both | Non-defective) = 0.95 x 0.98 = 0.931

P(Passes Both) = (0.02)(0.03) + (0.931)(0.97)
= 0.0006 + 0.90307
= 0.90367

P(Defective | Passes Both) = 0.0006 / 0.90367
= 60/90367
= 0.000664 (approximately 0.066%)

The two-stage quality control system is highly effective: only about 0.066% of items reaching the end of the line are defective, down from the original 3% defect rate.
